Family Health

A new breast lump, including near the bra line: what to do

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Finding a lump in either breast can be worrying. Many lumps have noncancerous causes, but a new lump should be checked wherever it appears: even directly under a bra band. Comfort measures can help while you arrange care; touch and location cannot reliably establish the diagnosis.

A new lump deserves an assessment wherever it is

A lump can occur in either breast, underneath it or near the place where a bra band or wire rests. Many causes are benign, meaning noncancerous, but its location does not tell you which cause applies. Arrange a medical appointment for a new lump even if it is small, moves under your fingers or does not hurt.

It helps to distinguish a spot in the skin from something deeper in the breast or chest wall, but you do not have to make that distinction yourself before asking for care. Avoid repeatedly pressing the area to test it. Tell the service that you have found a new breast or chest lump and mention any associated symptoms when booking.

Pressure and injury can change the area

A tight or poorly positioned bra can irritate skin or make an already tender area more noticeable. Changing the fit may improve comfort, but it does not establish the cause of a deeper lump. Do not postpone an examination simply because the lump sits directly beneath a seam or wire.

An injury or recent operation can leave a collection of blood called a haematoma. Damaged fatty tissue can also form a firm area known as fat necrosis. Tell the clinician about an accident, breast procedure or blood-thinning medicine. These explanations still need to fit the examination and, when appropriate, imaging; a remembered bump is not proof that every new mass is harmless.

1. An abscess is a collection of infected fluid

A breast abscess contains pus and may cause a painful lump, warmth, redness, fever or a generally unwell feeling. Redness can be less obvious on darker skin. Abscesses can occur during breastfeeding, often with mastitis, but they can also occur when a person is not breastfeeding.

A painful hot breast or suspected infection needs urgent advice. Ultrasound may help identify an abscess, and treatment can involve draining it with a needle or a small incision, with antibiotics when appropriate. Do not squeeze or puncture it at home. If symptoms worsen or fail to improve after treatment starts, contact the team again rather than waiting for a routine appointment.

2. A cyst is a fluid-filled structure

Breast cysts are common and can become tender or change with the menstrual cycle. A shallow cyst may feel smooth or soft, while a deeper one may seem firm. Those descriptions overlap with other conditions, so feeling the lump cannot confirm that it is a cyst.

Ultrasound can help distinguish fluid from solid tissue. A confirmed simple cyst may need no treatment; aspiration can sometimes relieve discomfort or help assess it. A complex appearance, bloody fluid, a remaining lump or other concerning finding can change the plan. Ask what type of cyst was identified and what change should prompt another visit.

3. Fibroadenomas are benign solid growths

A fibroadenoma often feels smooth, rubbery and mobile and is frequently found in younger people. It may be painless and can change with hormonal influences. The name describes a diagnosis, however, not something that can be confirmed because a lump moves when pressed.

Evaluation may include ultrasound and, in some circumstances, a needle biopsy. A confirmed fibroadenoma can often be monitored. Removal may be considered for growth, size, symptoms or uncertainty about the diagnosis, as well as individual preferences. Pain is not the only reason to review the plan, and surgery is not automatically necessary for every fibroadenoma.

4. Lipomas arise from fatty tissue

A lipoma is a benign fatty growth, often soft, slow-growing and movable under the skin. It may occur on the chest as it can elsewhere on the body. A clinician can assess whether the features fit that diagnosis and whether imaging or further investigation is needed.

Once confidently identified, an uncomplicated lipoma may simply be observed. Removal can be discussed if it is uncomfortable, changes, interferes with clothing or remains diagnostically uncertain. Do not label a new breast lump a lipoma solely because it feels soft: different types of masses can share that feature.

5. Breast cancer can appear in any part of the breast

Some studies find more cancers in the upper outer part of the breast, but cancer can occur near the bra line or elsewhere. A 2017 study of 110 patients found an upper-outer predominance; this pattern cannot be used to rule out a lower or inner lump. Right-sided and left-sided changes both deserve attention.

Cancerous lumps can be hard and fixed, but they do not always feel that way. Pain, softness or mobility cannot reliably exclude cancer. In a 2017 study of people diagnosed with breast cancer, a lump was the commonest presenting symptom, reported in about 83%. That does not mean that 83% of people who find a lump have cancer; those are different groups.

What survival figures can and cannot tell you

Finding cancer before it has spread can make treatment more effective. Current US SEER figures for female breast cancer diagnosed in 2016–2022 report five-year relative survival of 100.0%, rounded, for disease confined to its original site. Relative survival compares a group with similar people in the general population; it is not a promise that every individual is cured.

A population statistic cannot diagnose a lump or predict one person’s outcome. Tumour biology, stage, health and treatment all matter. Likewise, the proportion of biopsies that prove benign varies with who is referred and why. The useful response to a new lump is to arrange assessment, rather than trying to calculate a personal probability from a broad percentage.

6. Chest-wall inflammation can mimic breast-area pain

Costochondritis involves painful inflammation where ribs meet the breastbone. Movement, deep breathing or pressure may worsen the pain. Tietze syndrome is a related but distinct condition in which visible swelling can occur. Ordinary costochondritis does not usually produce that swelling, and neither diagnosis should be assumed to explain a new lump within breast tissue.

Chest strain, repeated coughing or an injury may be relevant, although a cause is not always clear. Once serious causes have been excluded, a clinician may advise activity adjustments and suitable pain relief. Anti-inflammatory medicine is not safe for everyone. New unexplained chest pain needs assessment, and sudden pain with breathlessness, faintness or spread to the arm or jaw requires emergency help.

Symptoms to mention when arranging the appointment

Report whether the lump is growing, whether skin is warm or red, and whether you have a fever. Also mention dimpling, a new change in breast shape, a nipple that has newly turned inward, a persistent nipple rash or unexpected discharge, particularly blood. A lump in the armpit is also worth reporting.

These changes can have causes other than cancer, but they help determine how quickly you should be seen. A new lump still needs checking when none of them is present. Seek urgent advice for a painful hot breast, fever or rapidly worsening swelling, and emergency help if you feel severely unwell or have concerning chest-pain symptoms.

Make the next step manageable

Choose comfortable clothing and reduce bra pressure if it irritates the area. A softer bra, a different size or a short break from wearing one may help with comfort. This is supportive care while arranging an appointment, not a treatment for an unexplained lump or a test of whether it is benign.

If you do not have a regular clinician, contact a local primary care clinic, community health service or breast service for the appropriate route. Explain that the concern is a new lump rather than a request for routine screening. Ask about access and timing if the first appointment offered is far away, especially if symptoms are changing.

Keep useful notes without repeatedly checking

Write down when you first noticed the lump, its approximate location, whether it seems to change and any associated pain or discharge. Include menstrual timing, pregnancy or breastfeeding, a recent injury, previous breast procedures, medicines and relevant family history. You do not need an exact measurement before seeking care.

Prepare a few questions: What is the likely explanation? Which test is needed and why? How will I receive the result? What should happen if it grows or remains noticeable? Consider bringing someone for support if you want to. Repeated squeezing or checking many times a day can increase soreness and worry without giving a dependable diagnosis.

Breast awareness complements screening

Becoming familiar with the usual look and feel of your breasts or chest can make a new change easier to notice. Texture can vary with the menstrual cycle and different life stages. Some health services suggest a monthly reminder, but do not wait for a scheduled check to report something new.

Self-checking cannot determine whether a lump is cancer and does not replace screening recommended for your age and risk. Conversely, a recent normal screening mammogram does not remove the need to investigate a new symptom. Tell the clinician when your last imaging took place and whether the current finding was present then.

The examination guides which imaging comes next

A clinician will ask about the change and examine the area, sometimes including the armpits. Ultrasound can distinguish fluid-filled and solid findings. For a younger patient it is often the first imaging test; diagnostic mammography or tomosynthesis is commonly used from age 30 onward, with ultrasound as needed. The exact plan depends on the individual situation.

Tell the team if you are pregnant or breastfeeding so the investigation can be adapted appropriately. MRI has selected uses but is not a routine first test for every lump. A chest X-ray, CT scan or general blood panel is not the standard way to rule out breast cancer. Blood tests may be useful for another suspected problem, such as infection.

A biopsy answers a different question from a scan

Imaging describes what an area looks like. If tissue confirmation is needed, a needle biopsy allows a pathologist to examine cells or tissue from the finding. Being referred for biopsy does not mean cancer has already been diagnosed, and many biopsies identify benign conditions. Ask how the procedure is done and when results are expected.

The examination, imaging and any tissue result need to make sense together. A normal scan is reassuring only in that context; a persistent suspicious lump may still need further investigation. If the result is described as probably benign, clarify the follow-up interval. Return sooner if the lump grows or symptoms change, and follow up if the promised result does not arrive.

After the result, agree a clear plan

The next step might be reassurance with specific return advice, follow-up imaging, treatment for infection, drainage of a cyst or abscess, or specialist treatment for another diagnosis. Ask for the name of the finding and the reason for the recommendation. A benign result can still require care if the lump is painful or changing.

If cancer is found, the breast team can explain its type and stage and discuss treatment options. You do not need to anticipate every possible treatment before the initial assessment. For now, the practical priorities are to arrange care, share the relevant history and make sure any result and follow-up plan reach you.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

New breast lumps need clinical assessment, with imaging and sometimes biopsy selected for the findings and individual circumstances.

Benign causes are common, but pain, mobility, bra-line location or a recent normal screen cannot independently exclude cancer.

How BeMama can help

Note when and where you found the change, report associated symptoms when booking, and agree how you will receive results and follow-up.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for a painful hot breast, fever or rapidly worsening swelling. Sudden chest pain with breathlessness or other emergency symptoms needs immediate help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Have a new lump checked in either breast, including near the bra line.
  • Abscesses, cysts, fibroadenomas and lipomas can require different care; they cannot all be identified by touch.
  • Changing a bra may improve irritation but does not diagnose a deeper mass.
  • Follow up a persistent or changing finding even after reassuring imaging.

Frequently asked questions

Can a tight bra explain a new breast lump?

It can cause pressure or skin irritation, but that does not establish the cause of a deeper lump. Improve comfort and arrange an assessment.

Is a lump below the breast less concerning than one near the armpit?

Location alone cannot rule cancer in or out. A new lump in either area should be checked.

If the lump moves and does not hurt, is it definitely benign?

No. Those features can occur with benign conditions but do not provide a dependable diagnosis. Examination and appropriate tests are needed.

Can a breast cyst feel hard?

A deeper cyst can feel firm. Ultrasound can help distinguish fluid from solid tissue; do not diagnose it by touch alone.

Do all fibroadenomas need surgery?

No. Some confirmed fibroadenomas are monitored. Growth, size, symptoms, uncertainty and preferences can influence whether removal is appropriate.

Should I squeeze a suspected abscess?

No. A painful hot lump or fever needs urgent advice. Drainage, when needed, should be performed by a healthcare professional.

Does costochondritis cause visible swelling?

It does not usually do so. Tietze syndrome can cause swelling at a rib-cartilage joint, but an unexplained breast lump or chest pain needs assessment rather than self-diagnosis.

Do I need a CT scan for a new lump?

Not routinely. Breast ultrasound and diagnostic mammography are common starting tests, selected for age and circumstances. A biopsy may be needed for tissue confirmation.

What if my recent mammogram was normal?

Report the new lump anyway. Screening and investigating a new symptom serve different purposes, and persistent findings may need further assessment even with normal imaging.

Does a 100% survival figure mean every early cancer is cured?

No. The rounded SEER figure is five-year relative survival for a defined population and diagnosis period. It is not an individual guarantee or a substitute for assessment and treatment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
